learn.title: 1. The First Americans: Origins & Cultures
learn.body:
Approximately 30,000 years ago, the Paleo-Indians—ancestors of all Native Americans—followed herds of animals from Siberia across Beringia, a land bridge connecting Asia and North America, into Alaska. By 8,000 BCE, these peoples had spread across North and South America.

Far from a "primitive" or sparsely populated land, pre-Columbian North America was home to millions. In 1492, at least 2,000 distinct languages were spoken across the Americas. Societies ranged from small hunter-gatherer bands to sophisticated urban civilizations, including the Mayas and Aztecs in Mesoamerica, the Incas in Peru, and the Moundbuilders and Mississippians in the Ohio and Mississippi River Valleys.

Native Americans cultivated plants for food, dyes, medicines, and textiles; built cities; developed communal land ownership; and constructed intricate systems of religious beliefs and political organization. After European contact, devastating epidemics—smallpox, typhus, measles, influenza—drastically reduced Native populations, greatly aiding European conquest.

learn.title: 2. Colonial Virginia: Labor, Servants & Slaves
learn.body:
From the earliest days of Jamestown (1607), labor was a major problem. After John Rolfe's successful cultivation of tobacco, the colony boomed—but demanded labor. The solution was indentured servitude: poor immigrants agreed to bind themselves for a set term (usually four years) in exchange for passage, food, clothing, and "freedom dues."

Large numbers of white indentured servants arrived until the 1680s. From the 1670s, the importation of African slaves swelled Virginia's labor force. Law increasingly distinguished between time-limited white servants and life-bound Black slaves. By the early 18th century, the largest landowners relied on enslaved labor, consolidating economic and political power.

learn.title: 3. Plymouth & Early Colonial Governance
learn.body:
In 1620, English Separatists (Pilgrims) arrived on the Mayflower at Plymouth, Massachusetts. While still aboard ship, they signed the Mayflower Compact—America's first document of democratic self-governance. The compact established rules for governing the new colony under Puritan religious values.

Plymouth grew as a center of Puritanism within the Massachusetts Bay Colony, though its political significance would eventually be eclipsed by Boston. Today it remains a major historical tourism destination, home to Plymouth Rock, the Mayflower II, and Plimoth Plantation.

learn.title: 4. Road to Revolution: Taxation & Resistance
learn.body:
Tensions between Britain and the colonies sharpened after 1763. The Stamp Act of 1765 required colonists to pay taxes on every page of printed paper to fund British troops. The colonial outcry centered on "no taxation without representation." Virginia's Patrick Henry articulated this in the Virginia Resolves, and nine colonies sent delegates to the Stamp Act Congress, which issued the Declaration of Rights and Grievances.

Boycotts forced repeal of the Stamp Act, but Parliament passed the Declaratory Act, asserting its right to tax the colonies as it saw fit. Key events escalating tensions included the Boston Massacre, the Boston Tea Party, and the Coercive Acts.

learn.title: 5. The American Revolution
learn.body:
The Revolution was the first modern revolution fought for rule of law, constitutional rights, and popular sovereignty. George Washington's leadership, French intervention (after the American victory at Saratoga, 1777), and British strategic errors turned the tide. In 1781, an American–French force defeated the British at the Battle of Yorktown. About 7,200 Americans died in battle; another 10,000 from disease and ~8,500 in British prisons.

Consequences were profound: Northern states began outlawing slavery or adopting gradual emancipation plans; new state constitutions guaranteed religious freedom and reformed tax and inheritance laws.

learn.title: 6. The Declaration of Independence
learn.body:
On June 7, 1776, Richard Henry Lee introduced the independence resolution. The Committee of Five—Adams, Franklin, Sherman, Livingston, and Thomas Jefferson—drafted the declaration. The Declaration had three parts: a natural rights theory statement; a list of grievances against King George III; and the formal declaration of independence. Jefferson drew on John Locke's natural rights philosophy and George Mason's Virginia Declaration of Rights.

Congress voted for independence on July 2, 1776 and adopted the Declaration on July 4, 1776. Notable changes during editing included removing Jefferson's condemnation of the slave trade.

learn.title: 7. The Articles of Confederation
learn.body:
Adopted by the Continental Congress on November 15, 1777, and ratified in 1781, the Articles of Confederation created a deliberately weak central government—a "league of friendship"—that preserved state power. There was no separate executive or judicial branch; Congress voted by state, with each state receiving one vote regardless of population.

Critical weaknesses: no power to tax, no power to regulate interstate commerce, and any amendment required unanimous approval—none were ever ratified. These flaws ultimately led to the Constitutional Convention of 1787.

anki.q: Where did Paleo-Indians originate, and how did they reach the Americas?
anki.a: They came from Siberia across Beringia (a land bridge connecting Asia and North America), arriving in Alaska approximately 30,000 years ago.

anki.q: By when had Paleo-Indians spread across all of North and South America?
anki.a: By 8,000 BCE.

anki.q: How many distinct languages were spoken in the Americas in 1492?
anki.a: At least 2,000 distinct languages.

anki.q: What was the basic principle of Native American land ownership?
anki.a: Land was held communally and worked collectively—private land ownership was a foreign concept.

anki.q: Name three major complex civilizations that developed in the pre-Columbian Americas.
anki.a: Mayas and Aztecs (Mesoamerica), Incas (Peru), Moundbuilders / Mississippians (Ohio and Mississippi River Valleys).

anki.q: Why were Native Americans so vulnerable to European diseases?
anki.a: They had no prior exposure to—and therefore no immunity against—diseases like smallpox, typhus, measles, and influenza that Europeans brought.

anki.q: What crop made Jamestown economically viable, and who successfully cultivated it?
anki.a: Tobacco, successfully cultivated by John Rolfe.

anki.q: What was indentured servitude, and what were the typical terms?
anki.a: A contract where a poor immigrant agreed to work for a master for a set term (usually 4 years) in exchange for passage, food, clothing, and freedom dues.

anki.q: Why did African slavery gradually replace white indentured servitude in Virginia from the 1670s onward?
anki.a: Enslaved Africans represented a lifetime of labor (long-term investment), legislation increasingly protected white servants while stripping rights from Black laborers, and elite planters could monopolize power through enslaved workforce ownership.

anki.q: What was the Mayflower Compact and why is it significant?
anki.a: Signed aboard the Mayflower in 1620, it was America's first document of democratic self-governance, establishing rules for Plymouth Colony.

anki.q: What was the core colonial argument against the Stamp Act?
anki.a: "No taxation without representation" — colonists argued only their own legislatures could tax them since they had no representatives in the British Parliament.

anki.q: What did the Stamp Act Congress produce in October 1765?
anki.a: The Declaration of Rights and Grievances, asserting that only colonial legislatures had the right to tax colonists.

anki.q: What was the Declaratory Act (1766)?
anki.a: Parliament's assertion, after repealing the Stamp Act, that it retained the right to legislate and tax the colonies in any manner it saw fit.

anki.q: What role did the Battle of Saratoga (1777) play in the Revolution?
anki.a: The American victory halted a British advance from Canada and persuaded France to intervene militarily on behalf of the colonies.

anki.q: What was the final major military engagement of the American Revolution?
anki.a: The Battle of Yorktown (1781), where an American–French force defeated the British.

anki.q: Who wrote the Declaration of Independence, and who were the other members of the Committee of Five?
anki.a: Thomas Jefferson wrote it. The Committee of Five also included John Adams, Benjamin Franklin, Roger Sherman, and Robert R. Livingston.

anki.q: What are the three structural parts of the Declaration of Independence?
anki.a: 1) A statement of natural rights theory; 2) A list of grievances against King George III; 3) The formal declaration of independence from Britain.

anki.q: On what date was the Declaration of Independence officially adopted?
What philosophical works influenced Jefferson's writing of the Declaration?
anki.a: John Locke's Two Treatises of Government and George Mason's Virginia Declaration of Rights.

anki.q: What were the key weaknesses of the Articles of Confederation?
anki.a: No power to tax; no power to regulate interstate commerce; no executive or judicial branch; each state had one vote; amendments required unanimous approval—none were ever ratified.

anki.q: When were the Articles of Confederation adopted and ratified?
anki.a: Adopted November 15, 1777; ratified by all states in 1781.

anki.q: What did the Articles of Confederation call the relationship between states?
anki.a: A "firm league of friendship" — it was a loose alliance that largely preserved state sovereignty.

anki.q: Approximately how many Americans died in the Revolutionary War, total across all causes?
anki.a: About 7,200 in battle, 10,000 from disease or exposure, and 8,500 in British prisons—roughly 25,000+ total.

anki.q: What was the impact of the Revolution on slavery in the North?
anki.a: Northern states began outlawing slavery outright or adopting gradual emancipation plans after the Revolution.

anki.q: What did Virginia Gazette runaway advertisements reveal about bound laborers?
anki.a: They showed that servants and slaves were highly skilled—carpenters, watermen, shoemakers, ironworkers—active in every phase of Virginia's economy, not just fieldwork.

quiz.q: Paleo-Indians arrived in North America by crossing which land bridge?
quiz.explanation: Paleo-Indians crossed Beringia, a land bridge connecting Siberia and Alaska, approximately 30,000 years ago.

quiz.q: What crop became the economic foundation of colonial Virginia?
quiz.explanation: John Rolfe's successful cultivation of a marketable tobacco strain made the colony profitable and fueled demand for bound labor.

quiz.q: What was the primary colonial argument against the Stamp Act?
quiz.explanation: Colonists argued that since they had no representatives in Parliament, Parliament had no right to tax them.

quiz.q: What American victory convinced France to enter the Revolutionary War?
quiz.explanation: The American victory at Saratoga in 1777 halted the British advance from Canada and led France to intervene on the colonists' side.

quiz.q: Who was the primary author of the Declaration of Independence?
quiz.explanation: The Committee of Five assigned the drafting task to Thomas Jefferson, whose writing was shaped by Locke and Mason.

quiz.q: Which of the following was NOT a weakness of the Articles of Confederation?
quiz.explanation: Each state had ONE vote (equal voting power). The real weaknesses were the inability to tax, no executive, and no commerce regulation.

quiz.q: The Mayflower Compact (1620) is historically significant because it was:
options: The first document granting religious freedom
America's first document of democratic self-governance
A peace treaty with Native Americans
quiz.explanation: The Mayflower Compact established rules for governing Plymouth Colony and is considered America's first document of democratic governance in the New World.

quiz.q: When did African slavery begin significantly replacing indentured servitude in Virginia?
quiz.explanation: From the 1670s, importation of African slaves swelled Virginia's labor force, and by the early 18th century enslaved labor dominated the largest plantations.
